title: Do Heat Pumps Cut Emissions on Today's Grid?

scenes.purpose: Pose the doubt the video tests.

visual.description: The question types on, large and centred; "cleaner" turns green as the sentence ends.
onScreenText: Is a heat pump really cleaner than gas?

scenes.direction: Cold open; hold half a second after the question mark lands.
scenes.narration: If the electricity that runs a heat pump comes from a gas or coal power plant, is the heat pump really any cleaner than the gas furnace it replaced?

scenes.purpose: Turn from the question to the evidence.

visual.description: Split field wipes the question away to an empty field ready for the first quote.

scenes.narration: It is a fair question, so let's put it to the studies.

scenes.purpose: Give the doubters' case in their own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "gas- and coal-fired" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "the majority of electricity in Massachusetts is sourced from gas- and coal-fired power plants"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; the second citation appears as the American Gas Association is named.
scenes.narration: The doubters are easy to find: one letter to the Boston Globe warned that "the majority of electricity in Massachusetts is sourced from gas- and coal-fired power plants", and the American Gas Association argues that a gas home can have a smaller carbon footprint than a heat pump home.

scenes.purpose: Give the counter-argument in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored from the previous one; "more heat energy" turns green as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "a heat pump can move more heat energy into a living space than the natural gas itself contains"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card.
scenes.narration: The channel Technology Connections answers that even with a gas-fired power plant behind it, "a heat pump can move more heat energy into a living space than the natural gas itself contains".

scenes.purpose: Set the test: real homes, real grids.

visual.description: The question types on centred; "real grids" holds in amber.
onScreenText: Which is it, on real grids?

scenes.direction: Hold one second before the investigation.
scenes.narration: So which is it, in real homes, on real grids?

scenes.purpose: Show the British result today, and keep the lifetime projection visibly separate.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars. The 36% bar grows on "36 percent" in solid green; the 68% bar grows on "68 percent" in a lighter hatched tone, labelled as a projection.

chart.title: Emissions cut after switching gas boiler to heat pump (UK households)
chart.note: The 68% assumes the grid keeps decarbonizing; only 36% describes today's grid.

citations.label: NBER working paper, UK heat pump households

scenes.direction: First bar on s07, second bar only on s08; camera punches on "not today's figure".
scenes.narration: Start in Britain, with households that replaced a gas boiler with a heat pump. A working paper turned the change in those households' energy use into emissions and found, in today's terms, a cut of 1.16 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per household per year: 36 percent of the footprint their energy use had before the heat pump. The authors also assume the electricity grid keeps getting cleaner, and on that assumption project a 68 percent cut across an assumed 20-year working life: a lifetime projection, not today's figure.

visual.description: The question types on; "coal" turns dark grey.
onScreenText: What happens where coal still runs the show?

scenes.narration: But not every grid is Britain's. What happens where coal still runs the show?

scenes.purpose: Show RMI's finding, including the Chicago exception, in its own words.

visual.description: The RMI passage on a page; the city names read in order, then the Chicago line highlights in amber as s11 is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: the short-term impact of electrification increases carbon emissions

citations.label: RMI, The Economics of Electrifying Buildings, 2018

scenes.direction: Highlight lands on "increased carbon emissions"; hold one second after s12.
scenes.narration: A report from RMI compared electric heating with gas in American cities on the grid of the time, and found it cut carbon in Oakland, Houston and Providence. But in Chicago, where coal is the power that answers extra demand most of the year, electrifying heat increased carbon emissions in the short term. RMI expected that to swing in favour of electrification, in Chicago and nationally, as coal plants keep retiring.

scenes.purpose: Give the summary figure, flagged as a summary.

visual.description: Title card; "20 to 30%" in green, large, "less carbon than gas furnaces" beneath.
onScreenText: 20 to 30% less carbon than gas furnaces

scenes.direction: Title lands on "20 to 30 percent"; dims slightly on s14.
scenes.narration: The Canadian Climate Institute, citing the International Energy Agency and a consulting firm, says that even on relatively emissions-intensive electricity, heat pumps emit 20 to 30 percent less carbon than gas furnaces, because they are so efficient. That is a summary of other work, not a measurement on any one grid, so it sits beside RMI's Chicago result rather than overturning it.

scenes.purpose: Ask how common the exception is.

onScreenText: How many homes sit on the wrong side?

scenes.narration: So how many American homes sit on the wrong side of that line?

scenes.purpose: Give the national estimate with its grid assumption beside it.

visual.description: Three tiles in a row: 2.1% lands first on "2.1 percent"; 45% and 15 years land together on "45 percent", in amber as assumptions.

chart.title: One US national model
chart.note: 2.1% is of all US houses, not gas homes alone, and depends on the grid getting cleaner.

citations.label: Deetjen et al., 2021, US housing stock model

scenes.narration: One national model found switching to a heat pump would raise CO2 emissions in just 2.1 percent of the US housing stock, a share of all houses rather than of gas homes alone, but that estimate assumes grid CO2 emissions fall 45 percent over the heat pump's 15-year life.

scenes.purpose: Show the national-lab result and what it does not measure.

visual.description: The passage on a page; the savings sentence highlights green on s25; on s26 "future grid" is underlined.

excerpt.highlight: Average annual GHG savings are positive in every state and in every heat

citations.label: Wilson et al., 2024, US national laboratories

scenes.direction: Hold half a second after s26.
scenes.narration: A second national study, from US national laboratories, modelled every home switching to a heat pump at once, not only gas-heated ones, and found average greenhouse gas savings positive in every state, in every future grid scenario it modelled, even the most conservative one. Notice what that measures: an average for each state on grids the authors project into the future, not today's grid, and not a count of the homes that come out behind.

scenes.purpose: State the pattern before its last piece of evidence.

onScreenText: The cleaner the grid, the bigger the gain

scenes.narration: The cleaner the grid, the bigger the gain.

scenes.purpose: Show the retrofit study's grid dependence in its own words.

visual.description: The LBNL passage on a page; the fuel-switching line highlights green on s16.

excerpt.highlight: the fuel switching dramatically boosted carbon reductions in this cluster

citations.label: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2021, retrofit study

scenes.direction: Hold one second before the answer.
scenes.narration: In a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study of home retrofits, the group of projects built around electrification, with solar panels, sat mostly in states with low-carbon electricity, and there switching fuels sharply boosted their carbon savings. The authors expect similar projects to save less carbon in states whose electricity is more carbon-intensive.

scenes.purpose: Give the answer in three lines.

visual.description: List builds one line per sentence: Britain in green, the Chicago exception in amber, the estimate caveat in grey.
onScreenText: British homes: about a third less
The exception: a grid like Chicago's

scenes.direction: Each line lands with its sentence; hold one second after the last.
scenes.narration: So does swapping gas for a heat pump cut emissions on today's grid? In the British homes, yes, by about a third of their energy footprint, and in RMI's words it already cuts carbon on today's grid in all but the most coal-heavy systems, though that was the grid when RMI wrote it. The exception is a grid like Chicago's. How rare that exception is, the evidence can only estimate: the national American studies both build in a grid that gets cleaner, so neither is a reading of today's grid alone.

scenes.purpose: Leave the viewer with the question to ask.

visual.description: The question types on centred; "when demand rises" in amber.
onScreenText: What does it burn when demand rises?

scenes.direction: Hold to the end; fade out.
scenes.narration: If carbon is why you are looking at a heat pump, the question to put to your power company is not whether it burns anything, but what it burns when demand rises, and whether that is changing. Know that, and you know the part of the answer these studies turn on.
